messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prison Guard
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Hopelessness: I have no future, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Alvarez was 28 when his younger brother died without warning. The call came on an ordinary workday while Mateo was finishing a shift as a prison guard. He had spent the morning walking the tier, listening to metal doors slam and inmates call out, and when he finally checked his phone in the staff corridor he saw several missed calls from family. By the time he reached his mother, his brother was already gone. In the first days after the death, Mateo kept replaying the fact that he had been at work, moving through his routine while his family was in crisis. What settled most heavily in him was not only the loss itself but the conviction that he should have protected his brother and failed. He spoke about it as if there had been some crucial moment he had missed, some action he should have taken, even when others told him there was nothing he could have done.

Before the death, Mateo described himself as easygoing and warm, the one in the family who joked first and tried to keep everyone steady. In the months that followed, he had come to believe that version of himself was gone. He told his wife that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable, and he said it with the flat certainty of someone no longer expecting to feel otherwise. The future, when he tried to imagine it, seemed blank. He was not describing dramatic plans or impulses so much as a deadened conviction that there was no real future waiting for him, only more days to get through.

His grief did not stay contained to private moments. It began to break into ordinary life in ways that frightened him. If a television in the break room showed a news story about a sudden death, or if an officer casually mentioned a local family losing someone, Mateo would feel the room start to shift. He would go strangely detached, as if the edges of things had gone unreal and he were no longer fully inside his own body. In those moments he often covered his face with both hands, pressing hard against his eyes and forehead, trying to block everything out until the sensation passed. He was embarrassed by this at work and started avoiding spaces where the news might be on or where coworkers tended to talk about tragedies in the community. In a prison setting, where conversation could be blunt and loss was common background material, that meant pulling away from the easy social contact he once had with other guards.

At home, avoidance took a quieter but equally rigid form. He sidestepped anything that reminded him of his brother. If his wife mentioned visiting Mateo’s mother and the conversation drifted toward family memories, he would leave the room or shut the subject down. He avoided photos, stories, and even ordinary references to people losing loved ones because he felt he could not get near those themes without the same unreal, detached feeling coming over him. His wife experienced him as absent and brittle. Arguments became more frequent, sometimes starting over trivial things—the dishes left out, a late text, a comment taken the wrong way. Mateo recognized, at least dimly, that he sometimes picked conflicts on purpose. The tension of fighting gave him something immediate to focus on, something hot and sharp that felt easier to manage than the hollow drop that came with grief.

Over time these habits began to shape his days. At work he kept his interactions narrow and functional. If the television in the control room was tuned to local news, he found reasons to step out. If another officer mentioned a funeral or someone’s bereavement, he stiffened, went quiet, and looked away. At home, his marriage narrowed around what could not be spoken. His wife wanted to remember his brother with him and could not understand why he seemed angrier the closer she came to the subject. Mateo, for his part, was certain that if he let himself go near the loss directly, he would come apart or disappear into that detached, unreal state.

What finally brought him to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of these moments. After recently covering his face in the staff area when a news segment about a family death came on, and then later starting another needless argument with his wife the same evening, he was shaken by how small his life had become. He said he felt miserable all the time and could not imagine this changing on its own. What frightened him most was the idea that this was permanent—that he had failed his brother, lost whatever future he once expected, and was now becoming someone unreachable to the people who loved him. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to stop feeling so unreal and to be able to hear his brother’s name without needing to hide from it.
